title: Mary, the Mother of Jesus
lead: Mary of Nazareth, the young Jewish woman who gave birth to Jesus. The Gospels tell of her faith at the angel's message, her presence at Cana and at the cross, and her prayer with the first believers. Christians agree that she is blessed, and differ on what else the church should believe about her and on whether to ask her prayers.

sections.b: Matthew and Luke both say that Mary conceived Jesus by the Holy Spirit while still a virgin (Matthew 1:18–25; Luke 1:26–38). In Luke she answers the angel with trust, visits her relative Elizabeth, and sings a song of praise, the Magnificat, in which she says every generation will call her blessed (Luke 1:39–56). She keeps and ponders what happens (Luke 2:19, 51) and hears Simeon say a sword will pierce her soul (Luke 2:35). In John she prompts Jesus's first sign at Cana (John 2:1–11) and stands by the cross, where Jesus gives her to the disciple he loved (John 19:25–27). Mark shows her family once trying to take Jesus home (Mark 3:21, 31–35). Acts places her in prayer with the apostles before Pentecost (Acts 1:14), and Paul says only that God's Son was "born of a woman" (Galatians 4:4).
sections.refs: Matthew 1:18–25; Luke 1:26–56; Luke 2:19–51; John 2:1–11; John 19:25–27; Mark 3:21–35; Acts 1:14; Galatians 4:4

sections.h: Old Testament pictures read as Mary
sections.b: From the second century, Christian writers read some Old Testament passages as pointing to Mary. Justin Martyr and Irenaeus set her beside Eve: Eve's disobedience brought death, and Mary's obedience opened the way to life. Others see her in the woman whose offspring crushes the snake (Genesis 3:15), in the queen mother seated at the king's right hand (1 Kings 2:19), in the ark of the covenant, since Luke's account of her visit to Elizabeth echoes David bringing the ark (2 Samuel 6:9–16; Luke 1:39–56), and in the woman clothed with the sun (Revelation 12:1–6). Many Protestant readers accept some of these as echoes but not as teaching about Mary; others read Genesis 3:15 and Revelation 12 as speaking first of Christ, Israel or the church. Isaiah 7:14 is quoted of the virgin birth (Matthew 1:23); its Hebrew word almah means a young woman, and the Septuagint, the Greek translation made before Jesus, rendered it "virgin."
sections.refs: Genesis 3:15; 1 Kings 2:19; 2 Samuel 6:9–16; Luke 1:39–56; Revelation 12:1–6; Isaiah 7:14; Matthew 1:23

sections.h: What the churches teach about Mary
sections.b: The Council of Ephesus (AD 431) called Mary Theotokos, "God-bearer" or Mother of God, to say that the child she bore was truly God. Most churches accept that title. Catholic teaching adds that she was kept free from original sin from her conception (the Immaculate Conception, defined in 1854), remained a virgin for life, and was taken body and soul into heaven (the Assumption, defined in 1950). Orthodox churches honor her as ever-virgin and celebrate her falling asleep, the Dormition, and her being taken to heaven, but do not accept the Immaculate Conception as Rome defines it. Luther, Zwingli and Wesley believed she stayed a virgin; most Protestants today think the brothers of Jesus were her later sons (Mark 6:3). Protestants honor her as a model of faith but reject doctrines about her that they do not find in Scripture.

Catholic and Orthodox Christians ask Mary to pray for them, as they ask any believer to pray, and honor her above all other saints. They point to Cana, where she brought a need to Jesus (John 2:3–5), and to Jesus giving her to the beloved disciple as mother (John 19:26–27). They say this honor is different in kind from the worship given to God alone. Lutheran, Reformed, Baptist, Pentecostal and most other Protestant churches do not pray to Mary. They hold that Christ is the one mediator (1 Timothy 2:5) and that Scripture gives no command or example of asking the departed for prayer. For the wider question, see The Saints and the Dead.

common: Christians agree that Mary conceived Jesus as a virgin by the Holy Spirit, as Matthew and Luke teach.
uncommon: Some Protestants, following Luther and Wesley, still hold that Mary remained a virgin all her life.
